summary:
Recent cybersecurity incidents have highlighted significant vulnerabilities across various sectors, including hospitality, critical infrastructure, and open-source AI platforms.

One notable incident involved Wyndham Hotels, which experienced a data breach due to a security flaw in its Android app. A security researcher discovered that a password embedded in the app's source code allowed unauthorized access to an internal database hosted by Salesforce. This breach potentially exposed personal information of millions of customers, including names, email addresses, and login tokens, although the exact number of affected records remains unclear. Wyndham has a large customer base, with approximately 129 million enrolled rewards members [Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse].

In another incident, a series of cyberattacks targeted refrigeration systems in French supermarkets, attributed to Iranian hackers. These attacks compromised digital thermostats, causing food spoilage by raising temperatures excessively. The French government has condemned these actions as unprecedented aggression and plans to impose sanctions against Iran in response to the attacks [Iran was behind cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers, Paris says].

Additionally, the cybersecurity landscape for open-source AI platforms is under threat. Recent attacks have targeted companies like Hugging Face and Fireworks, leading to unauthorized access to sensitive data, including API keys and customer information. These incidents underscore the risks associated with open AI platforms, which, while valuable for collaboration, may also expose vulnerabilities that can be exploited by malicious actors [Cyberattacks threaten to make open-source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns]. 

Overall, these incidents reflect ongoing challenges in cybersecurity, emphasizing the need for robust security measures across various industries to protect sensitive information and critical infrastructure.

article_hits.title: Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse
article_hits.content: Hotel and resort giant Wyndham has acknowledged a cybersecurity incident after a good-faith security researcher discovered a bug that allowed anyone to access customers’ personal information. Security researcher Robert Wiggins at What Security exclusively told TechCrunch that he found a password inside the source code of Wyndham’s Android app, which granted access to an internal company database, hosted by tech company Salesforce. Wiggins told TechCrunch that the credential exposed personal information including customer names, email addresses, and Wyndham member number. The database also stores customer login tokens ( called JWTs ) that keep customers logged-in to their apps without having to repeatedly enter their own passwords. The database also contained Wyndham files and documents. According to Wiggins, the database had millions of entries, but he was unable to determine an accurate number of exposed customer records. article_hits.title: Cyberattacks threaten to make open-source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns
article_hits.content: Loading the player… The very qualities that make open AI platforms valuable, like open doors and rich data, might also make them vulnerable to more hacks, Irene Solaiman, chief policy officer and SVP of strategy at Hugging Face said on a recent episode of the Equity podcast. The October attack on OpenCode , which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example. It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations. The risks aren’t limited to platforms that invite open community contributions. On Monday, AI infrastructure startup Fireworks, which helps developers run and train open AI models, disclosed that attackers had accessed some customers’ model weights, datasets, and billing information.
